title: Headache - what it is
text: A headache is pain or discomfort in the head, scalp, or neck. Common types include tension headaches, migraine, cluster headaches, sinus headaches, and headaches that begin in the neck. A mild headache can accompany a cold, the flu, or another viral illness along with a low fever.

title: Headache - call 911 / emergency room
text: Call 911 or go to the emergency room if: this is the first severe headache of your life and it interferes with daily activities; it started right after weightlifting, aerobics, jogging, or sex; it came on suddenly and is explosive or violent; it is the worst headache ever, even if you regularly get headaches; it comes with slurred speech, vision changes, trouble moving arms or legs, loss of balance, confusion, or memory loss; it is getting worse over 24 hours; it comes with fever, stiff neck, nausea, and vomiting; it occurs with a head injury; it is severe and in one eye only with redness in that eye; you are older than 50 and just started getting headaches; it comes with vision problems, pain while chewing, or weight loss; you have a history of cancer and a new headache; or your immune system is weakened by disease or medicines such as chemotherapy or steroids.

title: Headache - see a provider soon
text: See a provider soon if headaches wake you up or make it hard to fall asleep, a headache lasts more than a few days, headaches are worse in the morning, your usual headache pattern or intensity has changed, or you have headaches often with no known cause.

title: Tension headache - what it is
text: A tension headache causes pain or discomfort in the head, scalp, or neck, and happens when neck and scalp muscles tense or contract, often in response to stress, depression, a head injury, or anxiety. It is the most common type of headache and can occur at any age, though it is most common in teens and adults.

title: Tension headache - home care
text: What helps: hot or cold showers or baths; resting in a quiet room with a cool cloth on the forehead; gentle massage of head and neck muscles; relaxation techniques if stress or anxiety is a trigger; over-the-counter pain medicine such as aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, or acetaminophen; and avoiding smoking and alcohol. Taking pain medicine more than 3 days a week regularly can cause rebound headaches. Keep acetaminophen under 4,000 mg (4 g) a day to avoid liver damage, and avoid combining it with alcohol. A headache diary noting when pain began, food and drink over the past 24 hours, sleep, and activity right before onset can help identify triggers to discuss with a provider.

title: Tension headache - call 911
text: Call 911 if you are experiencing the worst headache of your life, you have speech, vision, or movement problems or loss of balance (especially if new for you), you have a fever with the headache, or it starts suddenly or is explosive in nature.

title: Tension headache - contact your provider
text: Contact your provider if your headache pattern or pain changes, treatments that used to work no longer help, you have side effects from medicine, you are pregnant or could become pregnant, you need pain medicine more than 3 days a week, or headaches are worse lying down.

title: Dehydration - what it is and causes
text: Dehydration occurs when the body does not have as much water and fluids as it needs. It ranges from mild to severe depending on how much fluid is lost or not replaced; severe dehydration is a life-threatening emergency. Common causes include sweating heavily, fever, vomiting or diarrhea, urinating too much, or simply not drinking enough due to illness, nausea, or a sore throat. Older adults and people with conditions like diabetes are at higher risk.

title: Dehydration - mild to moderate signs
text: Signs of mild to moderate dehydration include thirst, a dry or sticky mouth, reduced urination with darker yellow urine, dry and cool skin, headache, and muscle cramps.

title: Dehydration - severe signs
text: Signs of severe dehydration include no urination or very dark/amber urine, dry and shriveled skin, irritability or confusion, dizziness or lightheadedness, rapid heartbeat or breathing, sunken eyes, listlessness, shock, or unconsciousness. This level of dehydration is a medical emergency.

title: Dehydration - home care
text: For mild dehydration: sip water or suck on ice cubes, drink water or electrolyte sports drinks, and do not take salt tablets as they can cause serious complications. Ask a provider what to eat if diarrhea is involved. Dehydration from a stomach or intestinal virus should improve on its own within a few days. More severe dehydration or a heat emergency may require IV fluids in a hospital.

title: Dehydration - call 911
text: Call 911 or the local emergency number if the person loses consciousness at any time, there is any change in alertness such as confusion or seizures, fever is over 102F (38.8C), signs of heatstroke appear such as rapid pulse or rapid breathing, or the condition does not improve or gets worse despite treatment.

title: Dehydration - prevention
text: To prevent dehydration, drink plenty of fluids every day and more during hot weather or exercise. Pay close attention to fluid intake for sick family members, especially children and older adults, rather than waiting for signs of dehydration to appear. Anyone with fever, vomiting, or diarrhea should increase fluids right away.

title: Muscle aches - what they are and causes
text: Muscle aches and pains are common and can involve more than one muscle, as well as ligaments, tendons, and fascia. Pain is most often related to tension, overuse, or injury from exercise or hard physical work, usually starting during or just after the activity. It can also signal a body-wide condition such as an infection, including flu, or a connective-tissue disorder like lupus. Fibromyalgia, which causes tenderness in muscles and soft tissue along with sleep difficulty, fatigue, and headaches, is one common cause.

title: Muscle aches - home care
text: For muscle pain from overuse or injury: rest the affected area and take acetaminophen or ibuprofen. Apply ice for the first 24 to 72 hours after injury to reduce swelling, then switch to heat, which often soothes and may speed healing. Massage often helps overuse pain and fibromyalgia. Gentle stretching after a rest period and regular aerobic exercise such as walking, cycling, or swimming help restore muscle tone; start slowly and increase gradually, and avoid high-impact activity or weightlifting while in pain. Getting enough sleep and reducing stress, including through yoga or meditation, also helps. To lower future risk: stretch before and after exercise, warm up and cool down, stay hydrated around exercise, and stretch hourly if sitting most of the day.

title: Muscle aches - contact your provider
text: Contact your provider if muscle pain lasts more than 3 days, is severe and unexplained, shows signs of infection such as swelling or redness around the tender muscle, occurs in an area with poor circulation such as the legs, follows a tick bite or comes with a rash, or started or changed after beginning or changing a medicine dose such as a statin.

title: Muscle aches - call 911
text: Call 911 or the local emergency number if there is sudden weight gain, water retention, or urinating less than usual; shortness of breath or difficulty swallowing; muscle weakness or inability to move part of the body; or vomiting, a very stiff neck, or high fever.

title: Common cold - overview
text: Most people with cold symptoms such as runny nose, cough, and sore throat do not need specific treatment and can manage symptoms while preventing spread. Antibiotics are not appropriate for a typical cold and can cause side effects ranging from a rash to serious reactions or C. diff infection. If a provider diagnoses COVID-19 or flu, antiviral treatment may shorten symptoms and should ideally start within 5 to 7 days of COVID-19 symptoms or 2 days for flu. There are currently no antivirals for the other respiratory viruses that cause typical cold symptoms.

title: Common cold - managing symptoms (adults)
text: Get plenty of rest and drink plenty of fluids. Use a clean humidifier or cool mist vaporizer, saline nasal spray or drops, and breathe in steam from hot water or a shower. Throat lozenges or cough drops can help, and honey can ease cough for adults and children 1 year and older. Ask a provider or pharmacist about over-the-counter pain relievers or fever reducers, and mention any other medicines being taken.

title: Common cold - managing symptoms (children)
text: Over-the-counter cough and cold medicines are not recommended for children younger than 6 years old and can cause serious, sometimes life-threatening side effects. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever is appropriate with correct dosing from a provider. Do not give throat lozenges to children younger than 4, and never give honey to babies younger than 1 year old. A rubber suction bulb can help clear a young child's mucus, and sitting with a child in a steamy bathroom can ease congestion.

title: Common cold - when to seek medical care
text: Seek medical care if you or your child has trouble breathing or fast breathing, signs of dehydration, a fever lasting longer than 4 days, symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improving, symptoms that improve and then return or worsen, or a chronic condition that gets worse. Anyone at higher risk of severe illness from COVID-19 or flu should contact a provider right away even for mild symptoms, since early antiviral treatment works best. This list is not exhaustive; see a provider for any symptom that is severe or concerning.
